cleaned_segments.text: Anthony Bourdain graduated from the
Culinary Institute of America in 1978.
He was 21. His plan was to cook. So, he
cooked. Line cook jobs across New York
City, long shifts, loud kitchens, the
kind of work that pays just enough to
keep doing it. By the mid-1990s, he was
running the kitchen at Les Hall, a
French brasserie in Manhattan. Executive
chef. A career that from the outside
looked finished in the best possible
way. The problem was he also wanted to
be a writer. He tried twice. His first
novel, Bone in the Throat, came out in
1995. Almost completely ignored. His
second, Gone Bamboo, followed in 1997.
Same result. So, he kept
cooking. He ran his kitchen. He paid his
bills. And in 1999, he sat down and
wrote an essay about what professional
kitchens actually look like from the
inside. Blunt, funny, occasionally
disgusting. He called it Don't Eat
Before Reading This. It ended up at The
New Yorker. They published it. Kitchen
Confidential followed. Then No
Reservations. Then Parts Unknown. 18
years of traveling the world,
eating everything, talking to everyone.
A career that traced back entirely to
one moment where he sent something to a
place he wasn't sure he belonged.
What Bourdain did with that
career, and what he kept saying over and
over in different ways across 18 years
of television, was essentially one
argument. That the life most
people are carefully building for
themselves is missing the most important
thing. And that the most important thing
is almost always on the other side of
something uncomfortable.
Most people live inside a plan they
never actually made. A job that pays
well enough. A city they know how to
navigate. Restaurants they like. Routes
they've memorized. Routines that make
the days feel manageable. A life that
when you describe it to someone sounds
completely
fine. Fine is the word that keeps coming
up. And the thing about fine is it
doesn't alarm anyone. It doesn't raise
any flags. It's comfortable and clean
and completely sufficient, and it will
carry you from your 20s to your 50s
without ever once making you feel like
something is wrong right up until the
moment you realize that nothing
surprising has happened to you in years.
Most people plan the surprising out of
their lives without meaning to. They
make sensible choices. They take the job
that makes obvious sense instead of the
one they're not sure they can do. They
stay in the city where they already know
people instead of the one they've been
thinking about for 3 years. None of
these are bad decisions individually.
All of them stacked on top of each other
year after year quietly add up to a life
where nothing unexpected ever gets in.
Bourdain spent his 30s doing exactly
this. Good at his job. Had a title. Had
a kitchen that ran the way he wanted.
And two failed novels in a drawer
somewhere and a writing dream he'd
mostly made his peace with. From the
outside, it looked like a man who had
figured out what he was and accepted it.
What actually happened is that he got
bored enough to stop playing it
safe and do something that made no
obvious sense.
>> Be open to experience.
Be willing to try new things.
Don't have a rigid plan. Accept random
acts of hospitality without judgment or
fear. Don't be afraid to wander. Don't
be afraid to eat a bad meal. You
know, if you don't risk the bad meal,
you'll never get the magical
one. But I think most important, you
know, be humble. Be grateful. Be aware
of the fact that you are
probably the stupidest person in the
room.
As far as you are the least prepared,
least equipped person
to know
who's really in charge of what's really
going on.
>> The rigid plan is not just a travel
problem. It's the version of yourself
that already knows what you're capable
of and arranges your life accordingly.
It sets the ceiling before you've hit
it. It builds the box before you've run
out of room. And it does all of it with
perfectly reasonable justifications,
which is exactly what makes it so hard
to argue with. Bourdain's essay had no
business landing where it did. His
resume for that submission was two
novels nobody bought and 20 years of
cooking professionally. The New Yorker
published it anyway. The plan can't
account for the things that haven't
happened yet.
The bad meal is a specific concept. Take
risks. Step outside your comfort zone.
Embrace failure. All language that's
been said so many times it's become
background noise. Bourdain was not
talking abstractly. He was talking about
the fermented shark in Iceland that
smells like ammonia and tastes like
something that should not legally be
food. The unmarked restaurant
down the alley in Hanoi with no menu and
no prices and no clear indication that
what you're about to eat won't make you
sick for a week. Things he actually did
repeatedly on purpose because he
believed that the physical experience of
committing to something you weren't sure
about was the entire point. The bad meal
is not a metaphor for failure. It's a
metaphor for the moment before you know
how something is going to go. The job
you weren't sure you were qualified for.
The move to a city where you don't know
anyone. All of it lives in the same
category. All of it requires the same
thing, which is the willingness to eat
something before you know whether it's
going to be terrible or the best thing
you've ever tasted. Most people skip
this moment. They read the reviews
first. They eliminate as much
uncertainty as possible before
committing, which feels like wisdom and
is actually just a very sophisticated
way of making sure you never
accidentally stumble into something
extraordinary. Bourdain's career
is basically a long argument against
research. He showed up to places he knew
nothing about and figured it out from
there. He sat down at tables with people
whose names he couldn't pronounce in
languages he didn't speak
>> and ate whatever they put in front of
him. Not because he was fearless. He
talked about fear constantly, but
because he understood that fear was the
tax you paid on everything worth doing
and there was no way around it, only
through it. The thing he kept coming
back to was the idea that the experience
itself was the point, not the
destination, not the story you get to
tell afterward. The actual experience of
being somewhere unfamiliar and not
knowing how it was going to go. The bad
meal isn't something you survive on the
way to the good one. The bad meal is the
whole lesson. Discomfort is the
education.
>> If I do have any advice for anybody, any
final thought, if I'm an
advocate for anything, it's to move as
far as you can, as much as you can.
Across the ocean or simply across the
river. The extent to which you
can walk in somebody else's shoes or at
least eat their food, it's a plus for
everybody.
Open your mind.
Get up off the couch.
Move.
>> Most people are closer to the other side
of the world than they think. The
neighborhood they've driven past a
hundred times and never walked through.
The restaurant with no English menu. The
conversation they've been avoiding
because they already know it's going to
be uncomfortable. All of it is the other
side of the world. All of it requires
the same thing. The willingness to show
up somewhere you don't entirely know
what you're doing and stay long enough
to find out. Most people have already
decided how they feel about the places
they've never been, the food they've
never eaten, the people whose lives look
nothing like theirs. They formed that
opinion from a distance and they're
keeping it because going to actually
look means risking being wrong. And
being wrong about something you've held
on to for years is genuinely
uncomfortable. More uncomfortable,
honestly, than any bad meal. Anthony
Bourdain spent 18 years arguing against
this from every angle he could find. He
built an entire career out of showing
people what it actually looked like
inside the places they'd written off.
One table at a time, one meal at a time,
and he never stopped right up until he
did.
>> You're probably going to find
out about it anyway.
So, here's a little preemptive
truth-telling.
There's no happy ending.
